Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scans with thin cuts (<1 mm) are standard protocol to evaluate for areas of bony erosion, although findings typically demonstrate a non-specific soft tissue density with microcalcifications present in 20% of cases [19]. CT is particularly sensitive at detecting areas of hyperostosis, which has been used to predict the site of IP attachment with positive predictive values of 89–95% reported [20,21,22]. findings.evidence: Alternating lines of high and low signal intensity (convoluted cerebriform pattern) seen in an inverted papilloma of the maxillary sinus.

panels.rationale: Single coronal MRI of the sinonasal region. The caption explicitly identifies an inverted papilloma of the maxillary sinus and names the convoluted cerebriform pattern (alternating high/low signal lines), which is visible as the striated/columnar internal architecture within the left maxillary sinus mass. The in-text confirms CCP is a typical MRI finding of benign inverted papilloma. This is a real patient diagnostic image showing a specific manifestation of the configured target disease, so it is included; the cerebriform pattern is a classic presentation and is covered by the provided vocabulary.

in_text_mentions: ced or malignant-transformed forms, nasal endoscopy may reveal a polypoid, papillomatous, friable or bleeding mass, extending toward the choana, nasopharynx, maxillary sinus, ethmoid, frontal sinus, sphenoid sinus or skull base. CT and MRI are indispensable for assessing extension, bone remodeling or destruction, focal hyperostosis as an indicator of the attachment site, and the relationship with the orbit, skull base or neurovascular structures [17,18,19,20,21]. Endoscopic and CT features that suggest complex or potentially malignant disease are illustrated in Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3.

A nasal biopsy may sample only the papillomatous component and miss foci of minimally invasive carcinoma. For this reason, endoscopic, radiological and histological correlation is essential (Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4). Bone destruction, pain, significant epistaxis, rapid evolution or early recurrence should raise suspicion of malignant transformation even when the initial biopsy is benign. Conversely, focal hyperostosis may reflect the attachment site rather than malignant invasion; therefore, imaging interpretation must be integrated with histology and clinical context [17,18,19,20,21].

panels.attribution_text: Yan et al. Preoperative Prediction of Malignant Transformation of Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma Using MR Radiomics.. Frontiers in oncology 2022. doi:10.3389/fonc.2022.870544. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Patient 1: axial T1WI (A), axial T2WI (B), and axial contrast-enhanced T1WI (C). A 48-year-old man was pathologically diagnosed as inverted papilloma in the right nasal cavity and maxillary sinus, with severe epithelial atypical hyperplasia and carcinogenesis. The presence of convoluted cerebriform pattern and absence of extra-sinonasal involvement led to a misclassification as benign by the two radiologists, whereas the radiomic model well-classified it as malignant. Patient 2: axial T1WI (D), axial T2WI (E), and axial contrast-enhanced T1WI (F). A68 year-old man was pathologically diagnosed as an inverted papilloma in the left frontal sinus and, with squamous cell carcinoma in some areas. In this case, orbital invasion was a key feature of malignancy easily seen by radiologists. The two radiologists well-classified the case as malignant, whereas the radiomic model misclassified it as benign.
in_text_mentions: We also compared the performance of the two head and neck radiologists and the combined model ( Figure 4 ). As shown in Table 3 , the combined model had better accuracy (0.899) and sensitivity (0.828) than the two radiologists in the testing cohort. The specificity of the combined model was similar to the two radiologists. This indicated that the combined model could diagnose more patients with IP-SCC, while avoiding missed diagnoses.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Coronal enhanced CT from a case report of bilateral inverted papilloma (article title 'Bilateral endoscopic medial maxillectomy for bilateral inverted papilloma'; in-text: 'Biopsy revealed IP'). Real human-patient image showing a homogeneously enhancing mass filling the bilateral nasal cavities and maxillary/ethmoid sinuses with bone destruction of the right orbita. Bilateral disease makes this a variant (less common) presentation. Real human-patient image, no third-party restriction.

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology image at 25x from a human patient specimen showing the classic inverted growth pattern of Schneiderian papilloma: thickened pseudostratified ciliated epithelium invaginating into an underlying fibromyxoid stroma with cystic spaces and an intact basement membrane. The caption explicitly attributes these features to inverted Schneiderian papilloma, and the in-text description confirms endophytic growth of ciliated epithelium with mucous cells forming cystic spaces compatible with inverted Schneiderian papilloma. No carcinoma, dysplasia, or other disease is described for this panel (those are in Figures 3 and 4). No annotations, scale bars, or labels are overlaid on the image.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E histology at 40x magnification showing the classic endophytic/inverted growth pattern with thickened epithelial nests invaginating into the stroma, which is the hallmark histologic feature of sinonasal inverted papilloma. Real patient specimen from a pediatric case. B: H&E histology at 100x magnification confirming the endophytic growth pattern with benign non-keratinizing squamous epithelium, consistent with sinonasal inverted papilloma. Real patient specimen. C: H&E histology at 400x magnification showing uniform nuclei without cytologic atypia and intraepithelial neutrophils, which correspond to intraepithelial neutrophil microabscesses, a recognized histologic feature of sinonasal inverted papilloma. Real patient specimen.

Macroscopically, Oncocytic Schneiderian papillomas are papillary or polypoid lesions with a red to brown color. Nasoendoscopic examination revealed a right pinkish irregular nasal mass arising from the right middle meatus. A biopsy was taken, and a histopathological examination reported SNIP (Figure 1a). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of paranasal sinuses revealed a mass measuring 5.5 x 3.2 cm with extensive bony destruction with intraorbital extension and erosion of the lateral wall of the maxilla with extension to the cheek (Figure 2).

Microscopic description (Figure 1b) showed inverted papilloma composed of prominent downward endophytic growth of round elongated interconnected squamous and respiratory-type epithelial nests with smooth outer contour displaying adjacent malignant transformation. The malignant cells show moderate pleomorphism with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromatism, vesicular chromatin pattern, and prominent nucleoli. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 12 panels (A1, B1, C1, D1, E1, F1, A2, B2, C2, D2, E2, F2). A1: H&E low-power view of the second-surgery tumor showing the papillary/inverted growth pattern of oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma (a subtype of sinonasal inverted papilloma), supported by caption and in-text. B1: H&E medium-power view showing intraepithelial neutrophil microabscesses, a characteristic histologic feature of inverted papilloma, in the second-surgery tumor. C1: H&E high-power view of the OSP tumor showing a microabscess (blue arrow) plus scattered mucous cells and small cavities (red arrow), consistent with oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma histology. D1: Higher-magnification H&E view resolving the microabscess structure of the benign OSP component ('The structure is clearer under higher magnification'). E1: Ki67 immunohistochemistry of the benign OSP tumor showing a low proliferation index restricted to basal layer cells, supporting the non-malignant papilloma component. F1: p53...
panels.attribution_text: Zhang et al. Oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma-associated adenocarcinoma and KRAS mutation: A case report.. Medicine 2018. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000011025. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Pathological characteristics and immunohistochemical findings in the tumor in the second surgery. (A1) Low-power view showing the predominantly papillary surface pattern of the tumor. The cells are acidic. (B1) Medium-power view showing the microabscess structure of neutrophils with neatly arranged cells and no atypia. The blue arrow shows a microabscess and the red arrow indicates fibrous vascular axis. (C1) Scattered mucous cells and small cavities were visible under high-power view, and the cells were not heterotypic. The blue arrow shows a microabscess and the red arrow indicates a mucous cell. (D1) The structure is clearer under higher magnification. (E1) Ki67 staining of the tumor specimen. The proliferation index is low and only the basal layer cells are positive, indicating that the growth of the tumor is slow. (F1) p53 staining of the tumor specimen. Only the basal layer cells were positive, but the surface cells were negative, indicating that the cells were benign. Additional pathological characteristics and immunohistochemical findings in the tumor in the second surgery. (A2) Low-power view showing the predominantly papillary surface pattern of the tumor. Part of the tumor shows formation of small clusters, with crowded cells and the layered structure disappears. Visible infiltration of gland tubular structure in the stroma. (B2) Medium-power view showing glandular fusion, obvious cell atypia and visible nucleolus. The blue arrow shows a pathological mitosis-like nucleus, and the red arrow indicates necrosis/nuclear fragmentation. (C2) High-power view showing that the cells were crowded, disordered and heterotypic. (D2) Higher magnification of the mitotic-like nucleus. (E2) Ki67 staining indicated a high proliferation index. (F2) p53 staining of the tumor cells was positive, suggesting cell malignancy.

plate_findings.evidence: Caption (a): "Hyperplastic squamous epithelium growing endophytically"; in-text: "hyperplastic ribbons of basement membrane-enclosed epithelium growing endophytically".

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: H&E panel from the reported inverted papilloma showing endophytic growth arising from nasolacrimal duct epithelium, as stated in the caption and in-text; the nasolacrimal duct origin is a less common site. b: H&E panel from the same inverted papilloma shows foci of atypia interpreted as moderate dysplasia with no invasive malignancy; dysplasia is a clear caption manifestation not present in the allowed vocabulary. c: H&E panel showing the inverted/endophytic growth pattern of inverted papilloma, supported directly by the caption and in-text histology description. d: Immunohistochemistry panel from the same patient's papilloma shows p16 block positivity as stated in the caption; it is a patient pathology image, but the p16 finding is not represented in the allowed vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Walijee et al. Inverted Papilloma Originating Primarily from the Nasolacrimal Duct: A Case Report and Review of the Pertinent Literature.. Case reports in otolaryngology 2015. doi:10.1155/2015/123694. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: (a) Hyperplastic squamous epithelium growing endophytically. The inverted papilloma is seen to arise from nasolacrimal duct epithelium (arrow). Haematoxylin and Eosin, 20x. (b) Foci of atypia amounting to moderate dysplasia. No invasive malignancy is seen. Haematoxylin and Eosin, 40x. (c) Inverted pattern of growth. Haematoxylin and Eosin, 20x. (d) Immunohistochemistry for P16 showing block positivity. P16 IHC Syntech antibody, 20x.
in_text_mentions: Histological examination revealed hyperplastic ribbons of basement membrane-enclosed epithelium growing endophytically into the underlying stroma (Figures 4(a) and 4(c)). The epithelium is multilayered, 5–30 cell layers thick, and formed of squamous epithelial cells admixed with scattered mucocytes. Multiple foci of atypia, interpreted as moderate dysplasia, were reported with no overall evidence of invasive malignancy (Figure 4(b)). The patient was therefore a Krouse Stage 3 on the Krouse Staging System [4]. Immunohistochemistry was positive for p16 (Figure 4(d)).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Fused FDG-PET/CT of the head in a patient with oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma-associated adenocarcinoma shows a hypermetabolic soft-tissue mass in the left nasal cavity/nasopharynx; the CT component demonstrates the sinonasal mass, supporting attribution to sinonasal inverted papilloma. [raw subtype: oncocytic] B: Fused FDG-PET/CT showing an enlarged, hypermetabolic left submandibular lymph node, consistent with metastatic spread from the sinonasal papilloma-associated carcinoma; disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title and the panel-specific caption. [raw subtype: oncocytic]

panels.figure_caption: F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography/computed tomogramphy image before the fourth surgery. (A) The glucose metabolism of the left posterior nasal passages was increased (red arrow). The size of the mass was about 2.6 × 2.5 × 1.8 cm, and the density was not even. The CTavg was about 44 to 51 Hu and SUVmax 33 Hu. The radiation-uptake of the top of the left nasopharyngeal cavity was very thick; the size of the mass was about 2.5 × 2.4 × 1.7 cm, with CTavg about 45 to 53 Hu and SUVmax 45 Hu (blue arrow). (B) The enlarged lymph nodes in the left posterior mandible (black arrow) showed abnormal increase of glucose metabolism, about 2.2 × 2.0 × 1.8 cm and SUVmax 41 Hu. CTavg = computed tomography average value, SUVmax = maximum standard uptake values.

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel (x40) from a real patient. The caption explicitly identifies an inverted papilloma with papillomatous squamous epithelial proliferation and an endophytic growth pattern, matching the configured disease sinonasal_inverted_papilloma and the vocabulary finding of endophytic epithelial invagination. The article title (primary inverted papilloma of the middle ear) and in-text course (otorrhea, tympanoplasty, recurrence on MRI) support middle-ear origin, but the histologic pattern itself is the textbook inverted-papilloma appearance, so typicality is classic. No malignancy is stated, so no carcinoma finding is added; no microabscesses are captioned, so none are invented. No age, ethnicity, skin, or staging information is provided.

panels.rationale: Axial CT of the paranasal sinuses shows a large soft tissue density mass involving the nasal cavities and sinuses, with nasal septal destruction, maxillary ostial widening, and bone destruction. The caption and article title directly support sinonasal inverted papilloma, and the arrows mark the mass/septal destruction (red) and maxillary wall destruction (yellow). The finding vocabulary contains a unilateral CT mass key, but this lesion is mainly right-sided and bilateral, so it is tagged with the closest CT mass term and additional proposed findings.
panels.attribution_text: Kakkad et al. Inverted Papilloma From Nasal Septum: A Rare Case Presentation.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.48486. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT paranasal sinus (axial view) CT- Computed tomography A large soft tissue density mass lesion is seen in both nasal cavities, mainly in the right nasal cavity, resulting in near complete opacification with destruction of the nasal septum (red arrow) and widening of both maxillary ostia with destruction of right side maxillary wall (yellow arrow) and lamina papyracea. Complete opacification of all sinuses except left frontal sinus findings are suggestive of sinonasal mass as inverted papilloma.
in_text_mentions: Computed tomography (CT) of the paranasal sinuses (Figure 1) demonstrated near complete opacification of the nasal cavities, with the right nasal cavity being predominantly affected. The computed tomography (CT) scan also revealed destruction of the nasal septum, widening of the maxillary ostia, and near complete opacification of all sinuses except the left frontal sinus. No evident erosion of the sinus walls or intracranial extension was observed.

Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2021. doi:10.3390/diagnostics11101827. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: To characterize each component, an immunohistochemical examination was performed. The results of the immunohistochemical studies are illustrated in Figure 3. (Left column) The three components clearly showed differences in their immunoprofiles. SqCCis was diffusely cytoplasmic positive for pan-cytokeratin (CK) and nuclear positive for P40, but negative for the neuroendocrine markers CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. Conversely, the nests of atypical small cells were positive for CK with a perinuclear dot pattern and diffusely cytoplasmic positive for the neuroendocrine markers CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. (Middle column) However, the nests were negative for P40. (Right column) The anaplastic spindle cell lesion was negative for all markers. Based on the histologic features and the results of the immunohistochemical studies, a diagnosis of combined SNEC and sarcomatoid carcinoma arising in an inverted papilloma was rendered. It is important to distinguish whether a spindle cell lesion is another sarcoma or a spindle cell variant of SqCC (sarcomatoid carcinoma). A diagnosis of sarcomatoid carcinoma can be considered if the existing conventional squamous cell carcinoma is mixed with the spindle cell lesion or if the SqCCis is present together [8,9]. In our case, because the spindle cell component coexisted with SqCCis, we diagnosed this component as sarcomatoid carcinoma rather than another sarcoma. The original magnifications were 200×.
in_text_mentions: The stains used were hematoxylin and eosin stain (Figure 2 and Figure 3) and the polymer method (Figure 3). The original magnifications were 40× in Figure 2, 400× in the inset of Figure 2, and 200× in Figure 3.

panels.figure_caption: A 65-year-old male was referred to the department of otorhinolaryngology with epistaxis and right nasal obstruction for two months. His medical history revealed diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and pulmonary tuberculosis. (A) Physical examination demonstrated an easy-bleeding tumor in the right nasal cavity and bloody crust with an ulcerative lesion at the anterior septum; (B) The initial computed tomography (CT) showed a 4.5 cm × 3.4 cm × 4.8 cm soft tissue lesion infiltrating the right ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with destruction at the frontal sinus posterior wall and cribriform plate. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a residual mass with destruction in the posterior wall of the frontal sinus, cribriform plate, and dura invasion with suspicious brain parenchyma (right frontal lobe) invasion; (C,D) Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) showed a residual hypermetabolic mass involving the superior portion of the nasal cavity and the anterior portion of the ethmoid sinus, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 8.5. Clinical differential diagnoses included inverted papilloma with malignant transformation, lymphoma, and olfactory neuroblastoma. To confirm the diagnosis, an excisional biopsy was conducted.
in_text_mentions: After the biopsy, the patient underwent radiation therapy of 70.2 Gy. However, six months after surgical resection and radiation therapy, follow-up brain CT showed new round masses abutting the superior falx cerebri, left parietal lobe, and both frontal lobes (Figure 1D). The patient died later that month.

This is a classic textbook endoscopic presentation of sinonasal inverted papilloma. No patient age or ethnicity is stated, and the field shows nasal mucosa rather than skin, so skin_tone is null.

in_text_mentions: thogenesis of these tumors has not been clearly elucidated, but there is some evidence that suggests a potential role of inflammation as some IPs are associated with contralateral inflammation independent of the tumor on CT imaging [3,4]. As a result, the patient may have bilateral symptoms despite having an IP. This adds a diagnostic challenge as the presence of bilateral obstructive symptoms alone should not be used to rule out IP. Clinically, IPs can be distinguished from inflammatory polyps as they appear to be firm, non-translucent, and tend to have a poly-lobulated appearance (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: d maxillary sinuses were the most common sites for both tumor types. The SNIP tumors were mostly unilateral (7/8), and the SNIP-SCC tumors were both unilateral (4/8) and bilateral (4/8) (Figure 2 and Figure 3). Orbital or intracranial invasion was demonstrated only in SNIP-SCC tumors (2/8), one with intracranial invasion and one with both orbit and intracranial invasion (Figure 2). Only SNIP-SCC tumors demonstrated bone defects (6/8). The shape of the tumor was more often polypoid in the SNIP tumors (6/8) than in the SNIP-SCC (4/8). The surface of the SNIP and SNIP-SCC tumors was mainly rough.

panels.stage: malignant transformation (progression to squamous cell carcinoma)
panels.rationale: Single H&E histopathology panel (×100) from a real patient cohort, explicitly framed by the caption, article title ('Malignant transformation of sinonasal inverted papilloma') and in-text mention as the progression of sinonasal inverted papilloma to squamous cell carcinoma. The visible disordered papillary epithelium with loss of basement membrane, enlarged deeply chromatic nuclei, atypia and pathological nuclear fission directly demonstrates carcinoma ex papilloma, a specific manifestation of sinonasal inverted papilloma; not a diagram, control, animal, or other-disease panel. [raw subtype: malignant transformation (squamous cell carcinoma ex papilloma)]
panels.attribution_text: YU and LIU. Malignant transformation of sinonasal inverted papilloma: A retrospective analysis of 32 cases.. Oncology letters 2014. doi:10.3892/ol.2014.2539. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Representative image of the progression from sinonasal inverted papilloma to squamous cell carcinoma. The papillary epithelial cells exhibit a disordered arrangement, the basement membrane disappears, the nuclei are deeply stained and become larger, chromatin thickening with atypia is evident and pathological nuclear fission is visible (hematoxylin and eosin staining; magnification, ×100).
in_text_mentions: e analysis and comprised 25 males and seven females, with a male to female ratio of 3.6:1. The median age of onset was 56.5 years old. All 32 patients were diagnosed with pathologically malignant SNIP that had progressed to SCC (Fig. 1). Nasal inverted papilloma was the diagnosis in 18 patients, which included two cases of pathological nasal inverted papilloma dysplasia (Fig. 2), and the remaining 16 cases were of pathological nasal inverted papilloma with atypical hyperplasia (Fig. 3). In the present study, the corresponding incidence rates were 3.9% (14/356), and 5.1% (18/356), respectively.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Endoscopic view from a case of sinonasal inverted papilloma showing a polypoid/papillary intranasal mass, consistent with the classic endoscopic appearance of IP. Article title and in-text context confirm IP diagnosis. b: Axial CT of paranasal sinuses in a patient with sinonasal inverted papilloma demonstrating a unilateral sinonasal soft tissue mass, a classic CT feature of IP. Disease attribution supported by article title and in-text discussion of IP cases. c: Fused 18FDG-PET/CT image from Case 11 showing well-defined focal FDG uptake (SUVmax 5.6) in the sinonasal mass. In-text explicitly states well-defined areas of 18FDG uptake were observed in IP cases with SUVmax > 3. PET finding not in vocabulary so recorded as proposed finding.

in_text_mentions: The difference in the values of SUVmax⁡ between patients with diagnosis of IP and negative for IP was statistically significant (P = 0.0001). Comparing FDG-PET/CT findings with histological diagnosis, FDG-PET/CT revealed a sensitivity and specify of 100%, considering a SUVmax⁡ of <3.0 as a criterion for negative finding. Furthermore we noted that the cases with SUVmax⁡ < 3 showed diffuse 18FDG uptake (Figure 1), while well-defined areas of 18FDG uptake (Figure 2) could be observed in the cases with SUVmax⁡ > 3.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Human sinonasal inverted papilloma tissue stained for p27 by IHC; caption states 'p27 IHC (a) expression +++ ... in IPs' and the article focuses on inverted papilloma. The lobulated thickened epithelial nests surrounded by stroma display the endophytic invagination architecture characteristic of inverted papilloma, and strong brown nuclear p27 staining (+++) is visible, distinguishing this panel from panel b. b: Caption states 'p27 IHC ... (b) 0 in IPs'; this is the p27-negative comparator within the same sinonasal inverted papilloma study, i.e. a staining-level comparison of IP tissue, not a normal or control sample of another disease. The epithelial nests with inverted growth into the underlying stroma remain visible by counterstain, showing the endophytic invagination architecture of inverted papilloma, with absent brown nuclear p27 signal.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E of the patient's biopsy showing the diagnostic inverted (endophytic) epithelial growth into lamina propria/connective tissue, with the caption explicitly stating carcinoma cells infiltrating connective tissue. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title (inverted papilloma of the gingiva) and the specific captioned manifestation. Gingival site is a less common form, hence variant. B: Higher-power H&E of the same biopsy showing a concentric keratin pearl (pearl arrangement of keratinocytes), the cytologic correlate of the well-differentiated squamous carcinoma arising in the inverted papilloma that the article text explicitly documents. Same target disease as panel A; included as a real patient tissue image of the configured disease. C: Higher-power H&E of the same inverted-papilloma biopsy showing a keratin pearl with epitheliomatous giant cells at its periphery. The panel belongs to the target...

in_text_mentions: Sections from the biopsy tissue revealed surface dyskeratosis with underlying keratinocytic hyperplasia of the gingival epithelium. Basal and parabasal layers presented with epitheliomatous proliferation of cells with formation of giant cells. Retepegs were broadened and elongated with keratinocytes in a pearl arrangement forming the core and hyperplastic cells dotted by giant cells at the periphery [Figure 1]. At places, well to moderately differentiated squamous cells were seen in the parabasal layer and microinfiltrating the underlying connective tissue.

in_text_mentions: e analysis and comprised 25 males and seven females, with a male to female ratio of 3.6:1. The median age of onset was 56.5 years old. All 32 patients were diagnosed with pathologically malignant SNIP that had progressed to SCC (Fig. 1). Nasal inverted papilloma was the diagnosis in 18 patients, which included two cases of pathological nasal inverted papilloma dysplasia (Fig. 2), and the remaining 16 cases were of pathological nasal inverted papilloma with atypical hyperplasia (Fig. 3). In the present study, the corresponding incidence rates were 3.9% (14/356), and 5.1% (18/356), respectively.

plate_findings.evidence: soft masses in the posterior ethmoid sinuses (in-text mention linked to Figure 1)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Coronal CT in a patient whose biopsy confirmed an inverted papilloma (right papillary mass). The in-text explicitly attributes the sinus soft masses to Figure 1. Attribution to papilloma rather than the coexisting synovial sarcoma is uncertain because the article title names both diseases and the ethmoid finding is described only as edema; confidence is therefore moderate. B: Coronal CT showing bilateral sphenoid sinus soft tissue masses with bone absorption. The patient had a biopsy-proven inverted papilloma, and the sphenoid sinus is the article's stated site of the papilloma. However, bilateral sphenoid masses with bone destruction are more typical of the coexisting synovial sarcoma named in the article title, so disease attribution to papilloma is uncertain and confidence is low.

in_text_mentions: mass involving the sphenoid sinuses, nasal cavity and ethmoidal cells bilaterally. Cranially the tumor extended to the optic chiasm pushing apart optic nerves; it infiltrated the cavernous sinus on the left and the clivus posteriorly but no dural or brain invasion were documented. The tumor was also present in the posterior part of the left maxillary sinus and the nasopharynx (Figure 1A). A biopsy was taken and a histological examination was consistent with the diagnosis of IP with no dysplastic or malignant changes present (Figure 2). In situ hybridization for HPV 16/18 and 6/11 was negative.

panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced MRI coronal section of the head a) T1-weighted image. b) T2-weighted image. An irregularly shaped mass lesion is observed extending from the left frontal sinus to the ethmoid sinus. There is a convergence site of a gyri-like structure from the nasofrontal canal to the posterior wall of the frontal sinus, which is assumed to be the base. Abscess formation is observed in the orbit, intracranial epidural area, and left maxillary sinus with low signal at T1 and a mix of low and high signals at T2. The arrow indicates the base of the nasal sinus mass.
in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head (Figures 3a, 3b) revealed an irregularly shaped mass lesion extending from the left frontal sinus to the ethmoid sinus and a convergence area of gyri-like structures from the nasofrontal canal to the posterior wall of the frontal sinus was considered basal. Abscess formation was observed in the orbit, intracranial epidural area, and left maxillary sinus with low signal at T1 and high signal at T2.

in_text_mentions: team was included in the operation. All lesions were cleared, and total petrosectomy was performed. The damaged dura was repaired. The operation was terminated by obliterating the cavity containing the fat tissue. Pathologic evaluation of the specimen was reported as “IP-high grade squamous dysplasia” (Figure 6). The patient received a dose of 16 gy in 8 fractions. Radiotherapy could not be continued because of deterioration of the patient's general medical condition. General health problems worsened, and 4 months after the last operation, the patient passed away due to multiple organ failure.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of the third-surgery sinonasal tumor showing papillary epithelial fronds with cell congestion, consistent with the inverted/endophytic epithelial growth pattern of sinonasal inverted papilloma in this papilloma-associated adenocarcinoma case report. B: Medium-power H&E showing increased cell layers with crowded, heterotypic (obviously atypical) cells, the histologic hallmark of malignant transformation (adenocarcinoma) arising in the Schneiderian/inverted papilloma. [raw subtype: carcinoma_ex_papilloma] C: Immunohistochemistry of the third-surgery tumor showing negative CK5/6 squamous marker staining, supporting adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma arising in the inverted papilloma; no vocabulary key exists for IHC findings, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. [raw subtype: carcinoma_ex_papilloma] D: Immunohistochemistry showing diffuse brown CK7 positivity in the tumor cells, confirming adenocarcinoma...
panels.attribution_text: Zhang et al. Oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma-associated adenocarcinoma and KRAS mutation: A case report.. Medicine 2018. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000011025. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Pathological characteristics and immunohistochemical findings in the tumor in the third surgery. (A) Low-power view showing the predominantly papillary surface pattern of the tumor and cell congestion. (B) Medium-power view showing an increase in number of cell layers, and the cells were crowded and heterotypic. (C) Negative staining for the CK5/6 squamous cell carcinoma markers. (D) Positive staining for the CK7 adenocarcinoma markers.
in_text_mentions: At the third resection, observation under low magnification showed the structure of the nipple and crowding of the cells. At medium magnification, the cell levels were increased; the cells were crowded and the cells were obviously heterotypic (Fig. 4). Immunohistochemistry for CK5/6 and p63 was negative, but CK7 staining was positive. Thus, the tumor was adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.

panels.rationale: Single coronal CT of the paranasal sinuses from a biopsy-proven case of bilateral simultaneous sinonasal inverted papilloma (disease-focused article title; in-text: biopsy of the polyps revealed bilateral inverted papilloma). The caption documents homogenous opacities filling both nasal cavities and the left maxillary, frontal and sphenoid sinuses, i.e. sinonasal soft-tissue opacification on CT; the left-sided sinus opacification supports the CT sinonasal-mass finding, while the bilateral nasal-capture component is added as a proposed finding because the vocabulary CT entry is unilateral. Bilateral simultaneous inverted papilloma is a recognized less-common (variant) presentation rather than the classic unilateral mass. Real patient diagnostic image (prior triage: keep, not third party), no normal/control or other-disease content. Only acquisition metadata (date/window text) is overlaid; no diagnostic arrows or markers. Age and ethnicity are not stated.

panels.body_site: right temporal bone (external auditory canal, middle ear, mastoid)
panels.rationale: Single axial temporal CT from a human patient in a case report titled 'Malignant Transformation of Temporal Bone Schneiderian Papilloma Associated with HPV-6'. The image visibly shows unilateral complete opacification of the right external auditory canal, middle ear and mastoid by soft tissue mass, matching the caption and in-text description of a mass filling the right external auditory canal with mastoid penetration. Schneiderian papilloma in the temporal bone is a recognized but uncommon presentation of sinonasal inverted papilloma, so typicality is variant. The panel is a real patient radiology image showing a specific manifestation of the configured disease, not a diagram, control, other-disease panel or third-party image. No skin is shown and no age or ethnicity is stated. Orientation marker and scale are visible on the image. Malignant transformation in this article was histological and is not demonstrable on this CT, so no subtype is assigned.

panels.attribution_text: Zhang et al. Oncocytic Schneiderian papilloma-associated adenocarcinoma and KRAS mutation: A case report.. Medicine 2018. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000011025. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Pathological characteristics and immunohistochemical findings in the tumor in the fourth surgery. Metastasis tumor of cervical lymph nodes after the fourth operation. (A) Low-power view showing, in some regions, a solid arrangement of tumor cells and a low differentiated carcinoma structure. (B) High-power view showing obvious cell atypia. (C) Positive CK7 adenocarcinoma marker staining. (D) Ki67 staining indicated a high proliferation index, indicating actively proliferating cancer cells. (E) CK5/6 and (F) p63 stainings in the tumor showed negative staining for squamous cell carcinoma markers. (G) The blue arrow shows metastasis of the tumor in the marginal sinus of the lymph node. The red arrow indicates residual lymphoid tissue. (H) The blue arrow indicates a small number of tumor cells that are arranged in a gland tubular structure. The red arrow indicates that most of the tumor cells are flaky. (I) The nucleus is large, and it is vacuolated and polymorphous. The nucleoli are obvious, and mitotic image is visible. The blue arrow shows a mitotic image.
in_text_mentions: At the fourth resection (Fig. 5), low magnification images revealed interstitial infiltration of the gland ducts and the fibrous connective tissue around the ducts. In some regions, there was a solid arrangement of tumor cells and a low-differentiated carcinoma structure. There was obvious cell atypia under high magnification. Immunohistochemistry for CK5/6 and p63 was negative and staining for CK7 was positive. Immunohistochemistry for Ki67 showed that the proliferation index was high and the cancer cells were actively proliferating.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Preoperative axial T1 MRI from a case report titled 'Occult recurrence of sinonasal inverted papilloma masked by a mucocele'; the lesion is a unilateral left frontal/ethmoid mass ultimately diagnosed as SNIP. No cerebriform pattern is described and the scan was initially read as a mucocele, so the MRI appearance is atypical. B: Axial contrast-enhanced T1 MRI of the same unilateral left frontal/ethmoid lesion in the SNIP recurrence case. Peripheral rim enhancement without a solid cerebriform component led to an initial mucocele misreading, making this an atypical SNIP MRI presentation. C: Coronal contrast-enhanced T1 MRI showing the unilateral left sinonasal mass with orbital extension in the SNIP recurrence case report; rim enhancement and globe sparing mimic a mucocele, an atypical SNIP pattern. D: Sagittal contrast-enhanced T1 MRI of the same unilateral left frontal/ethmoid lesion in the occult SNIP recurrence; the...
panels.attribution_text: Wu et al. Occult recurrence of sinonasal inverted papilloma masked by a mucocele: a case report.. Frontiers in allergy 2026. doi:10.3389/falgy.2026.1877618. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative MRI of the left frontal and ethmoid sinuses. (A) Axial T1-weighted image shows a well-defined, isointense lesion in the left frontal and ethmoid sinuses, with bony defect of the left medial orbital wall and mass effect on the medial rectus muscle. (B) Axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image demonstrates low-to-intermediate signal intensity with peripheral rim enhancement, well-defined margins, persistent medial orbital wall defect, and medial rectus compression. (C) Coronal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image shows the lesion protruding into the left orbit, with peripheral rim enhancement and no invasion of the globe. (D) Sagittal contrast-enhanced T1-weighted image confirms similar features: well-defined borders, low-to-intermediate signal, and rim enhancement. (E) Axial fat-suppressed T2-weighted image reveals high signal intensity of the lesion, well-defined margins, medial orbital wall defect, and medial rectus compression. (F) Coronal fat-suppressed T2-weighted image shows the high-signal lesion extending into the orbit without globe invasion.
in_text_mentions: On T1-weighted images the lesion was isointense; on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images it showed peripheral rim enhancement without a definitely identifiable solid component; and on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images it was hyperintense. These findings were initially interpreted as a benign mucocele (Figure 3). A preoperative biopsy of the left middle meatal lesion showed no evidence of SNIP (Figure 2). These findings were initially interpreted as mucoceles. Given the patient's history of high-risk SNIP (Krouse stage T3) and persistent orbital symptoms, endoscopic sinus surgery was performed.

inage and partial lamina papyracea defect was identified. At the left frontal recess and frontal sinus ostium, a broad-based, friable, papillomatous lesion that bled easily was observed (Figure 4). Intraoperative frozen section confirmed the diagnosis of SNIP with focal mild cytologic atypia (Figure 2). Therefore, attachment-oriented radical resection was performed: the precise mucosal attachment site at the frontal recess was excised, the underlying bone drilled and cauterized, and the frontal sinus widely marsupialized (Draf IIb). Paraffin section pathology confirmed SNIP as well (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single axial post-contrast T1-weighted MRI from a case report titled 'A rare case of primary inverted papilloma of the middle ear.' The caption states MRI revealed a tissue process occupying the left middle ear in T1 isosignal, and the in-text adds T2 isosignal with contrast uptake and a perioperative biopsy consistent with inverted papilloma. This is a real patient radiology image directly attributed to sinonasal inverted papilloma (primary middle-ear presentation), so disease attribution is strong. The cerebriform pattern is used as the characteristic MRI manifestation of inverted papilloma; it is not explicitly worded in the caption and is not independently resolvable at this resolution, which lowers confidence. No panel letter is printed, so the single image is panel A. No age, ethnicity, skin, or staging information is provided; the image carries no annotations.
